chunks: What happens when you press the shutter. The question: How does a smartphone take pictures? Describe what happens when you press the button?
(and also before you press the button!)
When you press the shutter, the camera is not starting from scratch. It has been running since you opened the app.
The sensor streams frames, the phone keeps adjusting exposure, focus and color, and it stores the most recent frames.
The press just tells the phone to pick frames, then process and save them.
Think of a dash cam. It records nonstop and keeps only the last short stretch of footage. When something happens, it saves what was just recorded, not what comes after.
A phone camera with zero shutter lag works the same way: it holds the last few full-size frames, so the photo can come from the moment you pressed.
The dash cam does not show the live adjusting of exposure and focus, which keeps running in the background.
Sensor to ISP to DRAM is the data path; the statistics, firmware and registers form the control path.
The IMU provides motion data for exposure planning and stabilization ("OIS vs EIS image stabilization").
Preview stream: the continuous, lower-resolution frames that fill your screen and feed the automatic controls.
3 amps: auto exposure, auto focus and auto white balance, updated from each frame. Ring buffer: memory that holds the last few frames and overwrites the oldest.
Zero shutter lag (ZSL): taking the photo from frames already in the buffer, so there is no wait after the press. ISP: the block that turns raw sensor data into a finished image.
A 12-megapixel sensor at 10 bits per pixel makes a raw frame of about 15 MB. At 30 frames per second, a new frame arrives every 33 milliseconds. Keep the last 8 frames in memory.
That takes 8 times 15 MB, which is 120 MB, and holds about 267 milliseconds of history. You tap the button.
The phone picks the sharpest of those recent frames, runs the full image processing on it, then saves it as a compressed JPEG file. That is the whole idea.

"Before the press, the sensor streams continuously over MIPI, the ISP makes the preview and statistics, and firmware closes three loops: auto exposure, autofocus and white balance, while face detection runs and a ring buffer holds recent full-resolution frames for zero shutter lag.

On the press, the phone locks focus and exposure, chooses or captures frames, merges them in raw if it's HDR or night, runs the full ISP, encodes to JPEG or HEIC with metadata, and saves it, while the UI stays responsive."
